svg.aria-label: The difference between online password guessing, which is slow and noisy, and offline hash cracking, which is fast and silent once the attacker has stolen the hashes.
svg.title: Online guessing vs offline cracking — why stealing the hash changes everything
svg.text: ONLINE GUESSING — against the live system
The attacker submits guesses to the real login.
try "Summer2026!" → rejected → try again…
• SLOW — the server answers one try at a time
• NOISY — every failure is logged (Event 4625)
• STOPPABLE — lockouts, rate-limits, MFA, alerts
Defender's advantage: you SEE it and can throttle it.
OFFLINE CRACKING — after the hash is stolen
Attacker already has the hashes (NTDS.dit, LSASS,
/etc/shadow) and cracks them on THEIR own hardware.
• FAST — a GPU rig tries billions/sec (hashcat)
• SILENT — nothing hits your logs; no lockout applies
Once the hash is out, your login-side defences no longer apply.
WHAT DECIDES IF OFFLINE CRACKING WINS
FAST, unsalted hashes fall fast
NTLM, MD5, SHA1 — designed to be quick, so a GPU
runs through dictionaries + rules in minutes. Identical
passwords share a hash, so rainbow tables pre-compute them.
SLOW, SALTED hashes resist
bcrypt, scrypt, argon2 are deliberately slow, and a per-
password SALT makes identical passwords hash differently —
defeating rainbow tables and forcing one slow guess at a time.
…which is why the real defences are upstream
Stop the hash theft (protect LSASS/NTDS), use long unique
passwords a dictionary can't reach, and add MFA so a
cracked password still isn't enough to log in.
